publicDigest selects `recipient` (store.js:75), the notified party's address.

findings.title: Webhook signature verification is skipped when the header is absent
findings.evidence: The whole verification block - drift check and signatureMatches - is inside `if (header) { ... }` (lines 44-54), where header is `request.headers[config.webhook.header]`. When the header is not sent, the body is processed unconditionally (lines 56-59). The comment on lines 42-43 gives the reason: 'Older provider accounts have not been migrated to signed callbacks yet, so only enforce the signature once the provider starts sending one.' The verification code itself is correct - constant-time compare, length check, timestamp tolerance - which is what makes the surrounding condition easy to read past.
findings.impact: Anyone can post arbitrary delivery receipts by simply omitting the signature header: `curl -X POST /hooks/deliveries -d '[{"id":"...","status":"delivered"}]'`. That writes into the deliveries table with an upsert on provider_id (store.js:85-92), so an attacker overwrites the recorded status of real deliveries - marking failures as delivered or the reverse - and corrupts whatever billing or retry logic reads that table. The route is also outside the API scope, so it has no rate limit either.
findings.recommendation: Require the signature unconditionally and reject callbacks without one. If unmigrated provider accounts genuinely exist, enumerate them and route them to a separate, IP-restricted endpoint with a deadline, rather than making the control opt-in for every caller.

triage.reason: Nothing else authenticates the route: webhookRoutes is registered outside apiScope (server.js:42) so the session hook does not run, and the handler reads no other credential.
The branch is unconditional application code, not gated by an environment flag or a build; PULSE_WEBHOOK_SECRET being configured does not make the header mandatory.
This is the WEB-27 shape read precisely: the control has a real rejecting branch, and the caller decides whether it runs. A control an attacker can opt out of is not a control.

findings.title: requireRole is decorated and never called, and is unreachable from the admin routes
findings.evidence: authPlugin decorates the instance with requireRole (auth.js:58-64). Grep across routes/, lib/ and server.js finds no call site. Worse, because it is decorated inside the apiScope plugin it exists only on that encapsulated instance, so the admin route file could not call it even if it tried - fastify.requireRole is undefined in adminRoutes' scope. The result is that DELETE /admin/tenants/:id and POST /admin/sessions/impersonate, the two most privileged operations in the service, have neither a session check nor a role check.
findings.impact: The service has no function-level authorization anywhere. Every route is either fully open or open to any session holder; the role field is read out of the database into request.user (auth.js:33) and never compared to anything. This is the WEB-23 shape: the mechanism exists, its presence reads as coverage, and it enforces nothing.
findings.recommendation: Call it. `fastify.requireRole(request, 'operator')` at the top of every admin handler, once adminRoutes is registered inside a scope where both the hook and the decorator exist. Add a test that asserts a member-role session receives 403 from each privileged route, so the absence cannot return silently.

triage.reason: No other authorization layer exists: no preHandler, no route-level config, no guard in lib/store.js.
The routes that need it ship - routes/admin.js is registered on line 38 of server.js. It is the control, not the vulnerable path, that is absent.
It is not redundant defence: with the admin scope unauthenticated, this would have been the only check standing.

findings.title: The error handler returns the raw exception message to the client
findings.evidence: `reply.code(err.statusCode || 500).send({ error: err.message })` for every unhandled error. Errors reaching it include pg driver errors from lib/store.js, whose messages carry SQL fragments, column names and syntax positions, and Node system errors carrying file paths.
findings.impact: Reconnaissance is cheap, and given the column-name injection in searchNotifications the returned message becomes a direct oracle: a syntax error names the position at which the injected fragment failed, which turns blind injection into error-based injection.
findings.recommendation: Return a generic message with a correlation id for any status of 500 or above, keep the detail in the server log (which the same handler already writes on line 47), and pass through only messages the application authored deliberately.

triage.reason: No filter sits between the thrown error and the response; the handler forwards err.message verbatim.
The handler is installed unconditionally in build() and is not gated on NODE_ENV.
Reported at low on its own, and noted as an amplifier of the injection finding rather than as a standalone high.

findings.title: The production API task role is granted AdministratorAccess
findings.evidence: tierPolicies maps `ops: 'AdministratorAccess'` (line 29), prod declares `apiTier: 'ops'` (line 68) with the comment 'the production API also exposes the maintenance commands the on-call runbooks use, so it runs on the ops tier', and attachTierPolicy resolves `cfg.tierPolicies[cfg.apiTier]` and attaches it to the role (service-role.ts:43-46). That role is the ECS task role of the internet-facing API container (api-stack.ts:33-46, taskRole: serviceRole.role), so the credential is delivered to the container through the task metadata endpoint. The standard tier is ReadOnlyAccess, itself account-wide read.
findings.impact: Any code execution or SSRF in the production API container yields AWS administrator credentials for account 000000000003 - create users, read every secret, delete every backup. The blast radius of one application bug becomes the whole account. The service's actual needs are already granted explicitly three lines above: grantArtifacts, grantQueue and database.secret.grantRead (api-stack.ts:39-41).
findings.recommendation: Delete attachTierPolicy from ServiceRole and rely on the explicit grants. Maintenance commands that need broader rights belong to a separate role a human assumes with MFA and a session policy, not to the long-running task role of an internet-facing service.

triage.reason: The unskippable layer that could compensate would be a permissions boundary, a session policy or an organization SCP, and none is declared anywhere in beacon-cdk - no iam.PermissionsBoundary, no aws_organizations resource, and cdk.json's `@aws-cdk/aws-iam:minimizePolicies` affects policy rendering rather than attached managed policies. INF-04 and INF-01 both direct that a guardrail not declared in the repository is not to be assumed.
Nothing bounds it: the role has no condition, no expiry and is assumed by every task in the service for as long as it runs (desiredCount 6 in prod).

findings.title: The shared artifact bucket grants anonymous read on every object in production
findings.evidence: When publicRead is set the construct replaces BLOCK_ALL with a BlockPublicAccess that leaves blockPublicPolicy and restrictPublicBuckets at false (lines 33-40), and then adds a bucket policy granting `s3:GetObject` to `new iam.AnyPrincipal()` on `this.bucket.arnForObjects('*')` - every object, not a prefix (lines 55-64). prod sets `assetsPublic: true` (environments.ts:64), and data-stack.ts:28-32 passes it as publicRead into the single bucket it creates, which the comment on lines 26-27 describes as holding 'the brand assets the CDN pulls, the rendered documents and the tenant data exports'.
findings.impact: Every rendered document and every tenant data export in production is world-readable to any unauthenticated caller who knows or guesses a key, with no signature and no expiry. The construct is written correctly - public reads are opt-in, and the doc comment says so - and the defect is in composing that opt-in with a bucket that holds customer data. Reading either file alone finds nothing.
findings.recommendation: Separate the buckets: a public assets bucket for the CDN origin, and a private bucket with BLOCK_ALL for rendered documents and exports. If they must share, scope the AnyPrincipal statement to an `assets/*` prefix and serve it through CloudFront with an origin access identity so the bucket itself stays blocked.

triage.reason: The intent stated on environments.ts:63 is 'The CDN pulls the shared brand assets straight from the origin' - brand assets. The grant is on arnForObjects('*'), so what is exposed is unbounded relative to that intent, and data-stack.ts:26-27 says what else is in there.
Tenant data exports and rendered documents are customer data by the repository's own description of the bucket.
No CloudFront distribution with an origin access identity appears in any stack; the bucket policy is the access control, and it grants AnyPrincipal.

findings.title: The artifact grant is issued with no prefix, covering the whole bucket
findings.evidence: grantArtifacts is declared with `prefix = ''` as a default and its doc comment instructs the caller: 'Pass the prefix the service writes under so the grant stays scoped to it' (service-role.ts:48-56). api-stack.ts:39 calls `grantArtifacts(serviceRole.role, props.artifacts.bucket)` with two arguments, so the statements resolve to `arnForObjects('*')` and `s3:prefix: ['*']` (lines 60, 67) - s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject on every object in the bucket.
findings.impact: The API task role can read, overwrite and delete every object the platform holds, including other services' artifacts and every tenant's data exports, in the bucket data-stack.ts describes as shared. The construct was written to prevent exactly this and the call site drops the argument that would have.
findings.recommendation: Pass the prefix: `grantArtifacts(serviceRole.role, props.artifacts.bucket, 'api/')`. Remove the default value so omitting it is a compile error rather than a silent widening, which is the change that makes the class unrepeatable.

triage.reason: The bucket policy does not narrow principal permissions - it only adds the anonymous read - and no permissions boundary is attached to the role.
The API's stated need is 'the documents it renders for tenants' (api-stack.ts:38), which is a prefix, not the bucket.
Reported at medium rather than informational because the same role already carries AdministratorAccess in prod - the two compound rather than cancel.

findings.title: The dev environment opens bastion SSH to the entire internet
findings.evidence: `adminCidrs: ['0.0.0.0/0']` for dev, against 203.0.113.0/24 for staging and two /24-and-smaller ranges for prod. NetworkStack iterates cfg.adminCidrs and adds an ingress rule per entry on TCP 22 to the bastion security group (network-stack.ts:52-58). The bastion group is in turn granted ingress to the database on 5432 (lines 81-85), and the field is documented as 'Ranges the operators reach the bastion from'.
findings.impact: In account 000000000001 the jump host accepts SSH from anywhere, and that host is the one path into the database security group. Combined with pickEnv's fallback below, this is also the configuration any deployment with an unrecognised BEACON_ENV synthesises.
findings.recommendation: Give dev a real range, or drop the bastion in dev in favour of SSM Session Manager, which needs no ingress rule at all. The value that must never be 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 should be asserted in a snapshot test over the synthesised template rather than left to review.

triage.reason: dev is a real deployed environment with its own account id (line 34) and is what pickEnv returns by default (line 83), so the configuration ships.

22 is not 443: the pack's own criterion is that management ports open to the world are a finding rather than a review item, and nothing narrows it - no NACL, no managed firewall is declared in the stack.

INF-04's own exculpation requires a NACL or managed firewall 'declared in the same repo', and states that if it is not declared it must not be assumed. beacon-cdk declares none: NetworkStack creates the VPC, three security groups and flow logs, and no ec2.NetworkAcl or firewall resource appears in any stack.

findings.title: pickEnv silently falls back to the dev configuration for any unknown value
findings.evidence: `return environments[name ?? ''] ?? dev;`. Any value that is not exactly 'dev', 'staging' or 'prod' - a typo, an empty string, an unset BEACON_ENV combined with an absent CDK context key - resolves to dev. bin/beacon.ts:14 passes `process.env.BEACON_ENV ?? app.node.tryGetContext('env')`, both of which can be undefined, and the comment on lines 12-13 records the fallback as intentional for a laptop synth.
findings.impact: The dev configuration is the most permissive one in the file: adminCidrs 0.0.0.0/0, assetsPublic true, ephemeral true (which turns on RemovalPolicy.DESTROY and autoDeleteObjects for the artifact bucket, disables RDS deletion protection and multi-AZ, and cuts backup retention to one day). A pipeline stage that fails to export BEACON_ENV deploys that set without any error, and the resulting stack names and account pin make the mistake easy to miss until a teardown destroys data.
findings.recommendation: Throw on an unrecognised or missing name. A configuration selector should fail closed; if a laptop default is wanted, require it to be requested explicitly (BEACON_ENV=dev) rather than inferred from absence.

triage.reason: The finding is about a default, not about an attacker-supplied value reaching a sink.
The intent stated in the comment is a laptop synth, but the function is the only selector and is also what the pipeline calls; nothing distinguishes the two cases at the point of the fallback.
The account pin limits which account is reached but not which settings are applied, so the permissive configuration is really deployed rather than merely printed.

findings.title: The database instance is declared publicly accessible
findings.evidence: `publiclyAccessible: true` on the rds.DatabaseInstance, with the comment on lines 58-59 giving the reason: 'The analytics warehouse lives in a separate account and pulls nightly over the public endpoint.' The same resource is placed in `vpcSubnets: { subnetType: ec2.SubnetType.PRIVATE_ISOLATED }` (line 48) and attached to databaseSg, which allows 5432 only from serviceSg and bastionSg (network-stack.ts:76-85).
findings.impact: The declaration contradicts the placement and the intent expressed everywhere else in the stack: a dedicated isolated subnet tier exists specifically to keep this instance off any routable path. Once the flag is set, the security group is the single control between the internet and the database - and in dev the bastion that is allowed through it accepts SSH from 0.0.0.0/0. Cross-account access from an analytics warehouse is a routing problem, not a reason to give a database a public endpoint.
findings.recommendation: Set publiclyAccessible: false and give the analytics account a VPC peering connection, a PrivateLink endpoint or a read replica in a subnet it can reach. If the flag stays, it must be paired with an explicit, narrow ingress rule for the warehouse's addresses rather than relying on the two internal groups.

triage.reason: databaseSg is real and restrictive, but it is then the only layer - and the isolated subnet placement, which would have been the second, is contradicted by the flag. A single control that a security-group edit can widen is not the unskippable layer FP-01 requires.
The stated bound is 'the analytics warehouse pulls nightly', and nothing in the stack expresses that bound - no source range, no condition, no separate endpoint.
Reported at medium rather than high because the security group does currently restrict ingress, and written down because the declared posture and the deployed posture disagree.

findings.title: The API container is configured with a wildcard CORS origin and credentials enabled
findings.evidence: The container environment sets `CORS_ALLOW_ORIGIN: '*'` and `CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS: 'true'` (lines 59-60), with the comment on lines 57-58 explaining that browsers hit the API from every tenant subdomain and from an embedded widget 'so the origin cannot be pinned'.
findings.impact: The two settings are contradictory: browsers reject a wildcard origin on a credentialed request, so either the API's CORS layer reflects the request Origin to make the pair work - in which case any site reads authenticated responses as the visiting user - or credentialed cross-origin calls fail and the configuration is a latent trap for whoever fixes them. Both outcomes are defects, and the second becomes the first the moment somebody makes the widget work.
findings.recommendation: Supply the list of permitted origins as configuration and have the API match against it exactly, emitting the matched origin plus Vary: Origin. If an embedded widget genuinely needs any origin, it must not be authenticated by an ambient credential - use a per-embed token in a header instead.

triage.reason: These are environment values consumed by the application's CORS layer; the sink is whatever beacon/api:1.12.0 does with them, and the pair only functions if that layer reflects the origin.

The container image beacon/api:1.12.0 is not in this repository, so I cannot read how it interprets the two variables. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN; what is established is that the stack instructs it to allow any origin with credentials.
The API is the front end for per-tenant data - it is granted the database secret and the artifact bucket on lines 39-41.

findings.title: The service security group accepts the task port from the entire VPC
findings.evidence: `this.serviceSg.addIngressRule(ec2.Peer.ipv4(this.vpc.vpcCidrBlock), ec2.Port.tcp(8080), 'load balancer to task')` - the rule's own description names the load balancer, and its peer is the whole VPC CIDR, which includes the three public subnets. The databaseSg immediately below uses the correct form, taking security groups as peers rather than CIDRs (lines 76-85), which shows the pattern was known.
findings.impact: Anything with an address in the VPC reaches the API tasks on 8080 directly, bypassing the ALB and therefore its dropInvalidHeaderFields setting, its TLS termination and any listener rule. That includes instances in the public subnets and anything an attacker lands in the VPC.
findings.recommendation: Peer on the load balancer's security group instead of the CIDR - create the ALB's group in the same stack, or use the ecs_patterns construct that wires the pair. The neighbouring databaseSg rules are the model.

triage.reason: The intended exposure is stated in the rule description - the load balancer - and the peer is broader than that intent by three subnet tiers.
The tasks run in PRIVATE_WITH_EGRESS subnets, which limits reachability from outside the VPC but not from inside it, and no NACL is declared.
Reported at low because it requires an existing foothold in the VPC, and written down because it removes the edge controls for anyone who has one.
